newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government rasies spectre of early poll.
newsitem.headline: Australian government rasies spectre of early poll.

text.p: The Australian government on Monday threatened an early election in its campaign to force opposition parties to approve controversial legislation.
But opposition parties dismissed the threat, citing the government's falling popularity, worsening internal ructions, and surging support for race politician Pauline Hanson.

The Liberal-National coalition threatened to dissolve parliament if the upper house Senate blocked labour reforms or the prime minister's plan to end a bitter land rights row between farmers and Aborigines.

"If the Senate is going to give us a hard time on sensible measures we are putting up then we are entitled to stockpile them as double dissolution triggers," Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said on Monday.
If the upper house rejects or changes a government bill twice then the government is entitled to dissolve both the lower and upper houses of parliament and call an election.

Reith's early poll threat echoes a similar warning at the weekend by Prime Minister John Howard to farmers. Howard implied he would call an early poll in order to pass his 10-point plan to end a bitter land rights row between farmers and Aborigines.
But the Labor opposition and the Australian Democrats, who can combine with other minor parties and independents in the Senate to block the government, dismissed the threats.
"This is the hoary old chestnut. We've heard this crying wolf, we have heard this so many times before," Democrats leader Cheryl Kernot said in a radio interview. "I don't believe them."
The next election is not due until early 1999.
If an early election was called opinion polls show Hanson's One Nation Party would probably win Senate seats at the expense of the government, further complicating the balance of power.

Minor parties win Senate places more easily in a double dissolution election, when the full 76-seat Senate faces re-election instead of half the chamber in a normal election, because of Australia's complex proportional voting system.
Polls show the government's popularity has fallen to its lowest since ousting Labor 14 months ago, with its gap over the opposition halving to about six percentage points.

A split has also emerged between Howard's Liberal Party and the rural-based Nationals over his handling of the land rights problem, known as the Wik issue after a court ruling that Aborigines had undefined right to land leased to farmers.
"There's no case for a double dissolution at the moment, on any front," opposition Labor deputy leader Gareth Evans said.
"The Wik issue is one that I thought the government would be most reluctant to have a double dissolution on, given the chaos within the coalition's own ranks on that."
The government is also dogged by a stubbornly high unemployment of about 8.7 percent.
"If Mr Howard wants to go early to the polls, it should be on his job creation record -- I'm sure the 802,300 Australians who are unemployed would judge him very harshly," Kernot said.
